title: The three treasures
hookLine: I have three treasures: compassion, frugality, and not daring to be first (Tao Te Ching 67)
carry: gentleness, economy, and not daring to be first

cards: Ask someone what they'd grab if the house were on fire, and you find out what they treasure. Photo albums. A grandmother's ring.
The laptop. The dog, first, obviously. In chapter sixty-seven of the Tao Te Ching, the speaker answers a version of that question.
The answer isn't a thing at all; it's three ways of carrying yourself through the world. And the third, at first hearing, sounds less like a treasure than a weakness.

teach.b: First, the list. In James Legge's translation: "The first is gentleness; the second is economy; and the third is shrinking from taking precedence of others."
Other translators say compassion, frugality, and not daring to be first in the world. Some readers hear in the first word a parent's tender love for a child.
The second may sound familiar: frugal living came up just over a week ago.
Second, each treasure opens a door. With gentleness, the chapter says, one can be brave. With economy, one can be generous.

By not pushing to the front, one can become the leader of others. Courage grows out of tenderness, generosity out of thrift, and the one who hangs back is the one others end up following. Third, the warning.
People now, the chapter says, give up gentleness and still try to be brave, give up economy and still try to be lavish, give up the back and push for the front.
It says plainly where that leads: to death. A stark line. Fourth, the last word goes to the first treasure.
Gentleness wins when it attacks and holds firm when it defends, and heaven guards a person with it.

Day to day, the three are small and practical: a softer tone with a tired kid, not buying the thing to prove something, letting the other car merge. None of them would need carrying out of a burning house.
Nobody can take them in the first place.

how: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching keep the three treasures of chapter sixty-seven, compassion, frugality and not pushing to be first, as a short daily checklist for how to carry themselves.

games.q: you want to be brave. chapter sixty-seven names where courage comes from. what is it?
games.why: the chapter says that with gentleness one can be brave, and that giving up gentleness while still trying to be brave leads to death.

practice: Hold each treasure for a few breaths, gentleness, then economy, then not pushing to be first, and ask where it could go today. Then choose the one that seems to have a place waiting for it.
Rest with it, the way you'd keep a hand on something precious in your pocket.

wordCard.voice: Three treasures. In chapter sixty-seven: gentleness, economy, and not daring to be first. Today's word.
